name: Letybo

lead: Letybo is a brand of letibotulinumtoxinA, a botulinum toxin type A injected by clinicians to soften frown lines. It was approved by the FDA for glabellar lines in February 2024.
Like other toxins it is temporary. It is discussed as one of several brands beyond the best-known names.

paras: The toxin blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, relaxing the injected muscle so overlying lines soften.
Reported effects include headache, eyelid and brow drooping and eyelid twitching. Botulinum toxins are prescription-only and carry class warnings about spread of toxin effect.

lead: Letybo is a brand of letibotulinumtoxinA, a botulinum toxin type A injectable. It is used to soften frown lines between the eyebrows (glabellar lines) and, in routine practice, in the upper face more broadly.[1][1] The US Food and Drug Administration approved it for glabellar lines in February 2024, according to Wikipedia.[1]

The same toxin is sold in Korea and other markets under the brand name Botulax. Wikipedia lists headache, drooping of the eyelid and brow, and eyelid twitching among its most common adverse effects.[1]
Published research on its aesthetic use includes observational studies of upper-face treatment and a registered comparison with other toxins for forehead lines.[2][3][4]

paras: Letybo is indicated in the US for temporary improvement of glabellar lines.[1] A 2025 real-world report examined a newer botulinum toxin A in routine upper-face practice for forehead lines, glabellar lines and crow's feet, with attention to the interplay of elevator and depressor muscles.[2] Two completed observational studies registered in 2025 and 2026 covered upper-face and periorbital treatment.[3][4]

Wikipedia reports that the most common effects are headache, eyelid and brow drooping, and eyelid twitching.[1] Botulinum toxins as a class carry warnings about spread of toxin effect from the injection site, which the FDA highlighted in 2008 and 2009.[1]

Botulinum toxin type A blocks release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, weakening the injected muscle.[1] A 2026 in silico modelling study compared excipients across six marketed toxin products, reflecting that formulations differ mainly in the stabilizers around the neurotoxin.[5]
In looksmaxxing discussion, newer and imported toxin brands are discussed as alternatives to the best-known brands.

A registered phase 4 study compared letibotulinum toxin A with other toxin products for forehead wrinkles, measuring safety, efficacy and diffusion in 20 adults. The 2025 clinical-practice report and the two completed non-interventional studies described above are small and observational.[2][3][4] The product's pivotal approval trials were not reviewed here.

timeline.event: FDA approves Letybo for glabellar lines.[1]
